newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-BELGIANS WIN HEARTS AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BELGIANS WIN HEARTS AT AUSTRALIAN OPEN.

text.p: Belgium bowed out of the Australian Open on Wednesday, but not before two of its slender fighters put their tiny nation on the map of world tennis.
Belgium's first ever women's quarter-finalists in a grand slam event, Dominique van Roost and Sabine Appelmans, have earned much more than headlines at home and praise from the crowd.
They have politely scattered the tournament's top seeds and, though they fell short of the semifinals, the pair have tugged Belgium out of the shadows of European tennis.

"A lot of people think Belgium is French or whatever. Sometimes you cannot even see the country on the map," van Roost said after a torn abdominal muscle forced her to forfeit her quarter-final to 14th seed Mary Joe Fernandez on Wednesday.
"I think now they know more about Belgium from the tennis."
Van Roost and Appelmans, seeded 16th at Melbourne Park, are among the more slightly-built players on the circuit but have shown they have the biggest hearts to reach the quarter-finals.

Van Roost has been cursed with pain from virtually the start of the tournament, beating world number two Arantxa Sanchez Vicario with an injured arm and then playing through back cramps to see off 15th seed Chanda Rubin in straight sets.
By the time she met Fernandez on Centre Court on Wednesday, van Roost's abdomen had been strapped with tape for a week.
But the burning pain became too much after she launched into an overhead smash at 0-3 down in the the second set.
"That was one ball too much," said van Roost, who knew this time no amount of courtside treatment would see her through.
"I think something extraordinary has happened to me here. I hope that this will take me forward and help me get higher up the rankings. Only good can come of it."
Van Roost and Appelmans, who calmly dispatched third seed Conchita Martinez at the weekend, have charmed the Melbourne Park crowd with their bright, unpretentious style.
They even reminded some dewy-eyed tennis commentators of another generation.
"Do you think it says that you can look feminine on the tennis court and still be a good player?" one asked.

"I think a lot are very feminine and everybody try to look good on the court," van Roost replied. "It's also important the way you look on the court and your attitude also -- try not to give too bad an attitude."
And yes, she added, "Some look very sexy in the dress, which is also nice."

Like van Roost, Appelmans has been flooded with messages of congratulation and praise from home, but the encouragement was not enough to push her past 1995 Australian Open champion Mary Pierce in a close quarter-final tussle on Tuesday.
Appelmans faltered in the final set, but was well satisfied with her career-best performance.
"I never gave up," Appelmans said later. "I think that's the most important thing when you're out there. You just give it everything until the end."
